notes.b: In science, a theory is a well-tested explanation, not a guess. Evolution by natural selection (the process by which better-suited individuals survive and reproduce more) meets every part of that definition.
points: Evolution by natural selection is a broad explanation of a huge range of observations, including the diversity of life, adaptation, shared features, the fossil record and the distribution of species, so one idea accounts for many different kinds of evidence.
It is supported by evidence from many independent sources and it makes testable predictions. It could be shown false by evidence, but no such evidence has been found.

It is falsifiable (open to being proved wrong). Finding fossils of mammals in rocks older than the first fish, or finding that the DNA of closely related species was no more similar than that of distant species, would contradict it.

The everyday meaning of theory (a guess or hunch) is not the scientific meaning. Saying evolution is only a theory misunderstands the word: in science, a theory is the highest status an explanation reaches.
The cell theory (all living things are made of cells) and the germ theory of disease (microorganisms cause many diseases) are theories in the same sense, and nobody calls them guesses.

Two parts should be distinguished. The fact of evolution is that living things have changed over time and share common ancestors, which the evidence shows directly. The theory of natural selection is the explanation of how that change happens.
notes.tip: If asked why evolution is a theory, link it to the features of a scientific theory: wide explanatory range, many independent lines of evidence, testable predictions and falsifiability. Never say a theory is just a guess.

notes.h: Why it is so widely accepted and tested
notes.b: Acceptance of evolution rests on how often it has been tested and how well it has survived. Each new kind of evidence was a chance for it to fail, and it did not.
points: It has been tested for over 160 years, since 1859 (the year Darwin published On the Origin of Species), by scientists in every field of biology, and also in geology, chemistry and physics, for example radiometric dating of the Earth.

Evidence that was not known to Darwin has confirmed it: genetics (Mendel's work, recognised from 1900), the structure of DNA (1953), molecular comparisons of DNA and proteins, and many transitional fossils (fossils showing features intermediate between two groups).
Each new kind of evidence could have contradicted the theory, and did not. This is why independent confirmation counts for so much.
Its predictions have been confirmed. Tiktaalik, a transitional fossil, was found in rocks of the age the theory predicted, and trees built from DNA match those built from anatomy.
Evolution can also be seen happening: bacteria evolve resistance to new antibiotics and insects evolve resistance to pesticides, as the theory predicts.

It is accepted by almost all biologists and by scientific academies around the world, and is the framework used in all biological research. Acceptance is based on evidence, not on authority or majority opinion.

Like all theories, it has been refined: it was combined with genetics into the modern synthesis. Scientists still debate details such as how fast evolution happens and the roles of chance and of epigenetics (chemical changes that switch genes on or off without changing the DNA sequence).
Debate about details within the theory is normal science, not doubt about evolution itself.
notes.tip: When asked why the theory is widely accepted, give several different kinds of evidence plus the long history of testing, and say that acceptance is based on evidence rather than authority.

notes.h: Lamarck's theory and why natural selection replaced it
notes.b: Darwin was not the first to propose that species change. Comparing his explanation with an earlier rival, Lamarck's, shows why natural selection is the better one.
points: Lamarck's theory (Jean-Baptiste Lamarck, 1809) said that organisms change during their lives through the use or disuse of body parts, and pass these acquired characteristics to their offspring. For example, giraffes stretching to reach leaves would have offspring with longer necks.

Acquired characteristics are not passed on through DNA, the molecule that carries inherited information, so they do not reach the next generation. A weightlifter's children are not born with large muscles.
In the 1880s August Weismann cut off the tails of mice over several generations, yet their offspring still had normal tails. This was direct evidence against inheritance of acquired characteristics.
Natural selection works with variation that already exists in a population, so it explains adaptation without any need for the organism to try. It is also supported by genetics.

Darwin's explanation of the giraffe: giraffes with slightly longer necks, through inherited variation, reached more food in times of shortage, so they survived and reproduced more and passed on the alleles (versions of a gene) for longer necks.
Epigenetic inheritance is a small, limited exception, in which some chemical changes to genes can be passed on. It does not restore Lamarck's theory.
notes.tip: To compare Darwin and Lamarck on a feature, state each explanation in order using the giraffe: Lamarck says stretching changes the individual and the change is inherited, Darwin says existing variation is selected. Mention the Weismann mice as evidence against Lamarck.

notes.h: Natural selection compared with special creation
notes.b: A scientific explanation has to be testable. Comparing natural selection with special creation shows why evolution counts as the best available explanation.
points: Special creation, the belief that species were created separately in their present forms, is a matter of religious faith rather than a scientific theory, because it makes no testable predictions.

Special creation does not explain the evidence, such as homologous structures (similar bone layouts in different species), vestigial structures (reduced structures with little or no use), the order of fossils, or the pattern of DNA similarity.
Many religious people and organisations accept evolution. Science and faith answer different kinds of questions, so accepting one does not require rejecting the other.
Evolution by natural selection explains all the evidence together, with one mechanism, and makes predictions. No other explanation does this, so it is the best available explanation.
notes.tip: Say special creation is not a scientific theory because it cannot be tested, and keep the wording respectful. Do not call it foolish.

notes.b: Evolution is not just something that happened in the distant past. It can be observed today, especially in organisms with short generations (so changes build up quickly) and large populations (so there is plenty of variation).
points: Examples of evolution observed now include antibiotic-resistant bacteria such as MRSA, the Galápagos finches' beaks after the 1977 drought, the peppered moth, and the new cordgrass species Spartina anglica.

Viruses evolve fast. New variants of the virus that causes COVID-19 (SARS-CoV-2), such as Delta and Omicron, spread because their mutations helped them spread or escape immunity, so vaccines were updated.
Flu vaccines are updated every year for the same reason: the flu viruses change, so last year's vaccine may no longer match.
Pests and weeds evolve resistance to the pesticides and herbicides used against them, because the few resistant individuals survive and breed.
Cancer cells in a tumour can evolve resistance to the drugs used to treat them, by the same process of selection.

Human activity is now a strong selection pressure (a factor that decides which individuals survive): antibiotic and pesticide use, climate change and habitat loss. Highly specialised species with slow reproduction are least able to evolve fast enough.
notes.tip: For evidence that evolution is still happening, name specific examples such as MRSA, the 1977 finches, the peppered moth, Spartina anglica or COVID-19 variants, and say how each shows selection acting.

notes.h: Evolution as the unifying idea of biology
notes.b: Evolution is the idea that ties the rest of biology together. The geneticist Theodosius Dobzhansky wrote in 1973 that “nothing in biology makes sense except in the light of evolution”.
points: It explains the unity of life (shared cells, DNA, genetic code and ATP, from common ancestry) and its diversity (adaptation and speciation, the formation of new species).
Classification: modern classification is based on evolutionary relationships (phylogeny), so species are grouped by how closely they are related, and new DNA evidence keeps refining it.
Form and function: it explains why structures suit their functions, since natural selection favoured individuals whose structures did the job better.

Genetics and technology: comparing the genomes (complete sets of DNA) of different species to find which genes are shared and what they do depends on evolutionary relationships. There is more on this in Bioinformatics: genome databases.

Limits of the theory: it explains how life changed and diversified once it existed. How the first living cells arose from non-living chemicals is a separate question, still being researched, and is not part of the theory of natural selection.
notes.tip: Give one idea for each area of importance you name, with an example, such as classification, form and function, or technology.

notes.h: Applications of the theory: health, farming and conservation
notes.b: Evolutionary thinking has practical uses. It helps people in medicine, agriculture and conservation to predict and manage change in living things.
points: Medicine and health: it guides the responsible use of antibiotics to slow resistance (antibiotic stewardship), the yearly updating of flu vaccines, the tracking of new virus variants, and the treatment of cancers that evolve drug resistance.
Because of shared ancestry, studies of other organisms can tell us about human biology and disease. For example, mice share many genes with humans.
Agriculture and food: selective breeding of crops and animals (artificial selection, where people choose which individuals breed), and managing pesticide use to slow resistance.
Keeping varied crop genes protects against disease, because a variable crop is unlikely to be wiped out by one pathogen. This is the lesson of the Irish potato.

Conservation and sustainability: it shows why genetic variation in a population matters for its survival when the environment changes, since some individuals may carry alleles that suit the new conditions.

Small, inbred populations of endangered species are at risk because they have little variation. Specialised species are vulnerable to climate change and habitat loss because they cannot adapt quickly.
notes.tip: When asked to discuss the importance of the theory, use examples from medicine, agriculture or conservation, and explain each with its evolutionary reason, such as resistance from selection or loss of variation.

keyTerms.definition: In science, the highest status an explanation reaches: a broad, well-tested explanation supported by many independent lines of evidence.
Able to be shown false by evidence; a scientific theory must be falsifiable.
The observation that living things have changed over time and share common ancestors.
A feature gained during an organism's life through use, disuse or environment, which is not inherited through DNA.
The belief that species were created separately in their present forms; not a scientific theory because it is not testable.
The passing on of gene activity changes without changes to the base sequence of DNA; a limited exception to the inheritance of acquired characteristics.
The responsible use of antibiotics to slow the evolution of resistance.

questions.prompt: Discuss the importance of the theory of evolution in understanding biology.
questions.model: Evolution is a unifying idea in biology: it explains the unity of life, such as shared cells, DNA, genetic code and ATP, from common ancestry, and its diversity through adaptation and speciation. It explains classification, since modern classification is based on evolutionary relationships, and it explains why structures suit their functions, since natural selection favoured individuals whose structures did the job better.
